title: Father of many nations (Genesis 17:5)
hookLine: a convert asks if he may pray "God of our fathers"; the answer starts with Abraham's new name

cards: More than eight hundred years ago, a man named Ovadiah sends a worried letter to Maimonides, the most well-known rabbi of his day. Ovadiah became Jewish as an adult. Now his teacher has told him something that stings.
When the prayers say our God and God of our fathers, Ovadiah should leave those words out. Abraham, Isaac and Jacob aren't his fathers. Can he say them or not?
Maimonides writes back, and his answer starts in the chapter just before the three strangers came, when Abram gets a new name.

teach.b: On day forty-three, by the time the strangers came, Abram was already Abraham. Here's where it happened.

God tells him, in the old Jewish Publication Society translation: "Neither shall thy name any more be called Abram, but thy name shall be Abraham; for the father of a multitude of nations have I made thee."
In Hebrew, av hamon goyim. Not the father of one family. The father of many.
The rabbis of the Jerusalem Talmud used that verse to settle a question much like Ovadiah's: may a convert say our fathers? Yes, they said, because Abraham was made a father to everyone who comes in.
Maimonides told Ovadiah the same, warmly and plainly. Say every word. Abraham is your father.
Don't think less of where you come from. And remember the boy in the idol shop from day thirty-eight. In the story, the first Jew had no Jewish parents at all.
So who counts as Jewish today?
The movements answer in different ways. Orthodox and Conservative Judaism count a person born to a Jewish mother, or someone who converts.
Reform and Reconstructionist Judaism also count the child of a Jewish father, when the child is raised Jewish. Conversions done in one movement aren't always accepted by another.
Those differences are real, people feel them deeply, and this path won't pretend to settle them.
On this path, there's no test at the door. One Jewish parent, two, or none. A partner, a convert, a grandchild who found a box of old photos, someone still unsure what they believe.
Whatever brought you, there's a seat for you here.

how: Converts to Judaism traditionally take a Hebrew name as a child of Abraham and Sarah, and say every word of the prayers, including our God and God of our fathers. Who counts as Jewish by birth differs between movements.

games.q: who said what — tap the pairs.

s: a convert has to skip "God of our fathers" in prayer
Maimonides told Ovadiah to say every word: Abraham is his father too.
every Jewish movement answers "who is a Jew" the same way
Orthodox and Conservative count the mother's line or conversion; Reform and Reconstructionist also count a Jewish father, with a Jewish upbringing.
in the story, Abraham had no Jewish parents
the midrash has him growing up in his father's idol shop.

games.q: you're Maimonides. a convert writes: my teacher says I can't pray "God of our fathers." what do you answer?
o: your teacher is right; skip those words.
say every word: Abraham is your father too.
say them silently, so no one hears.
games.why: Maimonides wrote that Ovadiah should say every word, because Abraham is a father to all who join, and told him not to think less of his own lineage.

practice: Think back to whatever first pointed you toward this path: a parent or a grandparent, a partner, a friend's seder, a question you couldn't shake, a name on a family tree.
Don't weigh whether it's a good enough reason; just let it come, and give it a moment of thanks. If you pray, you can thank God for the road; if not, notice that it led you here.

wordCard.voice: Ovadiah, the convert who asked Maimonides whether he could call Abraham his father, and was told to say every word: yes.

orig.note: Hebrew: father of a multitude of nations, the meaning given for Abraham's new name in Genesis 17:5.

carryVoice: Your line: no test at the door. Whatever road brought you here, it counts. See you tomorrow.
